newsitem.title: CHINA: China foreign direct investment seen in decline.
newsitem.headline: China foreign direct investment seen in decline.

text.p: Foreign direct investment into China is expected to decline by about US$2 billion this year from last year's record of US$42.35 billion, a senior economist of the Economist Intelligence Unit said on Tuesday.
"I don't expect it to collapse," Ken Davies, senior regional economist at the EIU told Reuters in an interview.
"FDI (into China) has now peaked and we can expect it to decline, but it will still remain very high."

There is little evidence that the drop indicates a new awareness of the poor profitability of business in China, he said. Instead, it seems to follow a rise in labour costs, particularly in southern China, and the relocation of investment into cheaper labour regions in places such as India.

"Also, looking to other places like Mexico, Latin America is becoming more interesting. Inflation is falling and politically it's more stable and more open. And it's nearer to the United States," he said. "People are starting to look elsewhere."
China said total FDI in 1995 was US$37.7 billion, up from US$33.7 billion in 1994, US$27.5 billion in 1993 and US$11 billion in 1992.
China's late paramount leader Deng Xioaping's statement "to get rich is glorious" in 1992 spurred a rapid increase in FDI from prior levels below US$5 billion.
Despite the rise in overall FDI to US$42.4 billion in 1996, the proportion of FDI as total fixed investment fell to US$12.7 billion from US$13.9 billion in 1995 and US$16.7 billion in 1994.
Davies attributed the continued rise in FDI despite the decline in fixed investment to a reinvestment of profits by foreign companies active in China.
Domestic fixed asset investment is now growing more quickly than foreign fixed asset investment, depsite the fact investment growth has been held back by the austerity program that started in 1993.

"Everyone assumes all investment (in China) is foreign investment, and it's not," he said. But analysing foreign direct investment in China is an inexact science, Davies said. In a July report, the International Monetary Fund allowed about US$17.8 billion for errors and ommissions in the 1995 figures.
"That indicated something strange was going on. It was widely assumed that the errors and ommissions figures has included round-trippers," Davies said.
Round-trippers are Chinese funds sent out of the country and then reinvested into China via Hong Kong to qualify for preferential tax treatment.
But the errors and ommissions figure could also include investment from Taiwan and overseas Chinese, some of the largest investors in the country. These investments are not always easy to identify.
